value.overview: The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is a medium-large tropical seabird of the family Procellariidae. It spends most of its life over warm ocean waters and comes ashore mainly to breed on islands. Its long, pointed, wedge-shaped tail and buoyant flight distinguish it from many other shearwaters. The species has both pale and dark plumage forms. It is widespread across tropical and subtropical parts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, including waters of the eastern tropical Pacific.
value.classification: The Wedge-tailed Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. Its scientific name is Ardenna pacifica; older sources may use Puffinus pacificus.
value.identification: This shearwater is about 38–45 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 1–1.1 m. It has a slender body, long narrow wings, a slim grayish bill, and a conspicuously long wedge-shaped tail. The common pale form is gray-brown above and whitish below, often with subtle pale feather edges on the back. The dark form is dark brown overall. In flight it combines shallow wingbeats with smooth, low glides over the sea.
value.rangeHabitat: Wedge-tailed Shearwaters breed on tropical and subtropical islands across the Indian and Pacific Oceans, usually in low coastal colonies. Outside the breeding season they occupy open ocean, often over warm waters and near productive areas where predatory fish, dolphins, or other seabirds concentrate prey. In Costa Rica, the species is a rare and irregular visitor to Pacific waters rather than a commonly encountered coastal bird. Documented records include offshore sightings and observations associated with marine-bird feeding activity, including the southern Pacific region near Golfo Dulce.
value.migrationStatus: The species disperses widely across tropical oceans after breeding, but its movements are better described as seasonal oceanic dispersal than as a single, well-defined migration route. In Costa Rica it occurs only sporadically in Pacific offshore waters, and it is not considered a regular land-based migrant or common coastal species.
value.breeding: Wedge-tailed Shearwaters breed colonially on islands, usually nesting in underground burrows, rocky cavities, or sheltered sites beneath vegetation. Pairs are generally monogamous and both adults help excavate the nest, incubate the egg, and feed the chick. One white egg is laid per breeding season. Incubation lasts about seven to nine weeks, and the chick remains in the burrow for approximately 15 weeks before fledging. Adults commonly visit colonies at night, when the birds are highly vocal.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish and squid, with crustaceans and other small marine animals also taken. Birds often forage where predatory fish drive prey toward the surface, and they may gather with terns, boobies, jaegers, dolphins, and other seabirds. They catch prey by flying low and dipping the head or bill into the water, but they also rest and feed while sitting on the ocean surface.
value.behavior: At sea, Wedge-tailed Shearwaters are usually seen singly or in feeding groups that can contain hundreds or more birds. Their flight is relaxed and buoyant, with stiff wingbeats followed by glides on slightly bowed wings. They are strong swimmers and spend little time on land except during breeding. Colonies are mainly nocturnal, and adults communicate with loud, drawn-out calls. The species is long-lived and typically begins breeding only after several years.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall global trend is not precisely quantified, although the species remains widespread and locally abundant. Trends can differ among breeding colonies.
